title: Munitions replenishment: the delivery schedule is set at motors, energetics, metal parts and seekers, not at the primes
map_limitation: Supplier-side EDGAR full-text search reaches only part of this chain: four of the eight links that carry tickers name non-SEC filers (BA.L, RHM.DE, 012450.KS, AVIO.MI), and the deepest four links (nitration-feedstocks, nozzle-ablatives, load-assemble-pack, dod-munitions-procurement) carry no example tickers at all because every operator the cited sources name at those stages is either a government plant (Holston, Radford, Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head) or a private firm (Repkon USA, Eurenco, Poland's Nitro-Chem, Nammo, Anduril, X-Bow, Ursa Major, Firehawk, Castelion, Prometheus Energetics). Government-owned contractor-operated capacity is unreachable through a brokerage account and is separated out here rather than assumed away. Four further limits to carry forward. First, ticker collision: BA on this map is Boeing (PAC-3 MSE radar seeker) and BA.L is BAE Systems plc (THAAD infrared seeker, Holston operator); they are different issuers on two links. Second, the map cannot state content per interceptor: no cited source discloses what fraction of an interceptor's price lands at the motor, the seeker or the energetics, so the chain shows sequence and scarcity, not dollar shares. Third, the depletion figures that motivate the occurrence are analyst and official estimates, not audited inventory counts, so the demand side is directionally sourced and quantitatively soft. Fourth, and against the thesis this map was built to test: CSIS says explicitly that ammonium perchlorate, the most-cited single point of failure, is NOT currently the binding constraint because AMPAC's capacity outpaces demand by a significant margin. That link is mapped as HIGH rather than CHOKE_POINT on the strength of its own source.

links.name: Nitration feedstock chemistry (ammonia, nitric and acetic acid, cellulose)
links.role: The commodity chemistry every military explosive and propellant is nitrated from: ammonia and nitric acid, acetic acid and acetic anhydride, and the cotton linters or wood pulp that become nitrocellulose, a plane where the largest producers sit in Asia rather than in the countries doing the replenishing.

bottleneck.note: Global commodity capacity is large, so the constraint is location and qualification rather than tonnage. No listed producer in the cited sources discloses defence energetics as a business, which is why this link carries no example tickers.

evidence.claim: Precursor chemistry for military energetics is concentrated in Asia: China alone now produces close to a third of the world's ammonia, and Asia, led by China, produces more than half of the world's acetic acid.
evidence.source_name: Modern War Institute at West Point (Bazilian and Isler), An Explosive Problem: Energetics, Supply Chain Fragility, and US Military Readiness
source_excerpt: China alone now produces close to a third of the world's ammonia
Asia, led by China, produces more than half of the world's acetic acid

evidence.claim: Nitrocellulose is the chemical backbone of modern artillery propellant, and much of the cotton linter trade that feeds European nitrocellulose flowed from China.
evidence.source_name: European Policy Centre (Kremidas-Courtney), Running on empty: the chemical shortage undermining European defence
source_excerpt: Nitrocellulose is the chemical backbone of modern artillery
much of this trade flowed from China, a country that is supporting Russia's war effort

capture_inputs.substitutability: Wood pulp is being researched as a substitute for cotton linters in nitrocellulose, so the feedstock is not permanently fixed [European Policy Centre, as of 2025-06-18].
capture_inputs.concentration: China produces close to a third of world ammonia and Asia more than half of world acetic acid [Modern War Institute, as of 2026-08-18].
capture_inputs.margin_posted_by: NULL: no cited source attributes margin at this stage to a named listed producer.

links.name: Energetic materials: RDX, HMX, IMX formulations, TNT and nitrocellulose
links.role: The nitration and crystallisation step that turns commodity chemistry into explosive and propellant material, run in the United States from a single surviving RDX site and supplemented by allied TNT imports, which is where the replenishment clock is set before any shell or warhead is filled.

bottleneck.note: One US site makes RDX, domestic TNT production was absent for decades, and an Army study puts seven years on making an energetics line worker fully effective, so this link cannot be surged with money alone.

evidence.claim: US commercial RDX production collapsed from five civilian plants with roughly 119 million pounds a year of capacity in 1980 to one site, Holston, producing under seven million pounds by 2006.
evidence.source_name: Modern War Institute at West Point (Bazilian and Isler), An Explosive Problem: Energetics, Supply Chain Fragility, and US Military Readiness
source_excerpt: Commercial RDX production once existed at five civilian plants in the USA, with a combined national capacity of roughly 119 million pounds a year in 1980.
By 2006 all of that had come down to one site, Holston, producing under seven million pounds.

evidence.claim: Holston is still the only place in the country that makes RDX.
evidence.source_name: Modern War Institute at West Point (Bazilian and Isler), An Explosive Problem: Energetics, Supply Chain Fragility, and US Military Readiness
source_excerpt: Eighty years later, the same site is still the only place in the country that makes it.

evidence.claim: BAE Systems has operated the Holston plant since 1999 and produces explosive fills such as RDX and HMX there for artillery and other munitions.
evidence.source_name: BAE Systems, Finalizing Major Modernization at Holston Army Ammunition Plant
source_excerpt: BAE Systems has been the operating contractor of the Holston plant since 1999

links.name: Ammonium perchlorate and composite propellant oxidiser
links.role: The non-substitutable oxidiser in the composite propellant of nearly every US and allied solid rocket motor, historically produced for defence by one qualified domestic manufacturer and now being expanded by its listed parent.

bottleneck.note: A textbook single point of failure that the best current source says is NOT the binding constraint: AMPAC's capacity outpaces demand by a significant margin, so the risk here is disruption and price setting, not throughput.

evidence.claim: Ammonium perchlorate is a non-substitutable propellant ingredient for nearly all US and allied solid rocket motor systems, and in the past only one qualified domestic manufacturer, American Pacific Corporation, produced it for defence applications.
evidence.source_name: CSIS Missile Defense Project (Rumbaugh and Karako), Solid Rocket Motors for Missile Defense: Challenges and Opportunities for Expanding the Industrial Base
source_excerpt: AP is a non-substitutable propellant ingredient for nearly all U.S. and allied SRM systems and serves as a case for understanding challenges with single points of failure.
In the past, only one qualified domestic manufacturer, American Pacific Corporation (AMPAC), produced AP for defense applications.

evidence.claim: Reliance on AMPAC alone is not currently a bottleneck in solid rocket motor production because the company's capacity outpaces demand by a significant margin, though a disruption could create industry-wide effects.
evidence.source_name: CSIS Missile Defense Project (Rumbaugh and Karako), Solid Rocket Motors for Missile Defense: Challenges and Opportunities for Expanding the Industrial Base
source_excerpt: While reliance on AMPAC alone for production of AP is not currently a bottleneck in the production of SRMs
the company's production capacity outpaces demand by a significant margin

evidence.source_name: CSIS Missile Defense Project (Rumbaugh and Karako), Solid Rocket Motors for Missile Defense: Challenges and Opportunities for Expanding the Industrial Base

links.name: Nozzle ablatives and insulation (rayon precursor and carbon materials)
links.role: The heat-protection materials in the solid rocket motor nozzle, whose defence demand is too small and too cyclical to keep a commercial line open, which is why suppliers left the industry and the government has repeatedly had to stockpile or subsidise it.

bottleneck.note: Not a capacity choke point today, but the clearest case in the chain of a material whose supply depends on a commercial market that has walked away. No listed supplier is named in any source fetched for this map, so the ticker list is deliberately empty.

evidence.claim: Rayon is a component of solid rocket motor nozzles that protects the aluminium structure from the heat of the expanding gases, and the industrial base has historically faced supply challenges with it.
evidence.source_name: CSIS Missile Defense Project (Rumbaugh and Karako), Solid Rocket Motors for Missile Defense: Challenges and Opportunities for Expanding the Industrial Base
source_excerpt: rayon, a component of SRM nozzles that helps protect the aluminum structure from the heat of the expanding gases
the industrial base has faced challenges with supply of rayon, a precursor to a component found in nozzles

evidence.claim: Rayon suppliers began to exit the industry in the 1990s once polyester displaced rayon commercially, prompting NASA to commission a stockpile of 2.5 million pounds of rayon fibre to support motor production through 2005.
evidence.source_name: CSIS Missile Defense Project (Rumbaugh and Karako), Solid Rocket Motors for Missile Defense: Challenges and Opportunities for Expanding the Industrial Base
source_excerpt: Without an alternative source of demand, rayon suppliers began to exit the industry in the 1990s.
prompted NASA to commission a stockpile of 2.5 million pounds of rayon fiber to support SRM production through 2005

evidence.claim: Rayon demand for defence applications is relatively low and cyclical and is not alone sufficient to make production profitable, so manufacturers have relied on commercial sales to keep lines open.
evidence.source_name: CSIS Missile Defense Project (Rumbaugh and Karako), Solid Rocket Motors for Missile Defense: Challenges and Opportunities for Expanding the Industrial Base
source_excerpt: Rayon demand for defense applications is relatively low and cyclical.
Alone, it is not sufficient to make production profitable, meaning that manufacturers have had to rely on commercial sales to keep lines open.

capture_inputs.substitutability: Rayon could not be easily replaced in motors, which is why a stockpile rather than a substitute was the answer [CSIS, as of 2026-06-12].
capture_inputs.margin_posted_by: NULL: no listed supplier is named in any source fetched for this map.

links.name: Seekers and terminal guidance sensors
links.role: The infrared and active radar seekers that make an interceptor hit rather than fly, each programme's seeker coming from one plant and one supplier, which is the sub-tier the Pentagon has had to sign multi-year framework agreements to widen.

bottleneck.note: Single-facility, single-supplier by programme: every PAC-3 MSE radar seeker from one Boeing plant in Huntsville, the THAAD infrared seeker from BAE Systems in Nashua and Endicott. Delivered volumes are in the hundreds against interceptor goals in the thousands.

evidence.claim: Every PAC-3 MSE active radar seeker comes from one Boeing facility in Huntsville, Alabama, which delivered only around 650 to 700 seekers in 2025.
evidence.source_name: Foreign Policy Research Institute (Amoah, Bazilian and Matisek), Scaling Patriot Production: The Industrial Base Crisis Explained
source_excerpt: Boeing produces the active radar seeker for every PAC-3 MSE from a single facility in Huntsville, Alabama, and in 2025 it delivered only around 650 to 700 seekers.

evidence.claim: BAE Systems signed a seven-year framework agreement with the Department of War to quadruple production capacity and accelerate delivery of the infrared seeker for the THAAD interceptor missile.
evidence.source_name: BAE Systems news release, BAE Systems and U.S. Department of War sign agreement to quadruple THAAD seeker production
source_excerpt: BAE Systems signed a landmark seven-year framework agreement with the Department of War to quadruple production capacity and accelerate delivery of the infrared seeker for the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor missile.
This new, multi-year agreement provides a long-term demand signal that gives us the confidence to further invest in expanding our capacity.

evidence.claim: BAE Systems' work on the THAAD seeker takes place at the company's facilities in Nashua, New Hampshire, and Endicott, New York.
evidence.source_name: BAE Systems news release, BAE Systems and U.S. Department of War sign agreement to quadruple THAAD seeker production
source_excerpt: BAE Systems' work on the THAAD seeker takes place at the company's state-of-the-art facilities in Nashua, New Hampshire, and Endicott, New York.

capture_inputs.concentration: One facility per programme: Boeing Huntsville for PAC-3 MSE, BAE Nashua and Endicott for THAAD [FPRI, as of 2026-05-18; BAE Systems, as of 2026-03-25].
capture_inputs.substitutability: A seeker is programme-specific and requalification-bound, so a second source is an agreement to build one, not a switch.
capture_inputs.margin_posted_by: NULL: both named seeker suppliers are diversified primes and no cited source breaks out seeker margin.

links.name: Solid rocket motor production

bottleneck.note: The bottleneck the whole sector names out loud. Two incumbents sit inside diversified primes and the pure-play entrants are private, so the listed way to own this link is not the same thing as owning the constraint.

evidence.claim: Solid rocket motors remain a bottleneck across the US missile industrial base, and between 2000 and 2015 the domestic industry shrank from six suppliers to two, Aerojet Rocketdyne and Orbital ATK, now part of L3Harris and Northrop Grumman.

links.name: Nondestructive inspection, test and requalification
links.role: The acceptance stage that decides whether a finished motor may ship: X-ray and a tailored set of inspections and tests, plus the requalification burden that fires whenever any upstream ingredient changes, which is the mechanism that turns a single supplier loss into a multi-year delay.

bottleneck.note: Runs inside the motor makers rather than as a purchasable service, so there is no listed way to own it. It matters because it converts an upstream substitution into a requalification of the propellant, the motor and the missile.

evidence.claim: The solid rocket motor manufacturing process comprises eight steps: propellant mixing, curing, casting, assembly, X-ray inspection, testing, coating and painting.
evidence.source_name: CSIS Missile Defense Project (Rumbaugh and Karako), Solid Rocket Motors for Missile Defense: Challenges and Opportunities for Expanding the Industrial Base
source_excerpt: The SRM manufacturing process is comprised of eight steps, each involving complex and specialized materials and sub-processes: propellant mixing, curing, casting, assembly, X-ray inspection, testing, coating, and painting.

evidence.claim: Before acceptance, solid rocket motors undergo a tailored set of inspections and tests, and internal defects can alter the burn pattern or create structural weaknesses.

links.name: Load, assemble and pack (warhead and shell filling)

notes.text: Thesis test, stated plainly because the map was built to test it rather than decorate it. The claim was that the choke point sits one and two tiers upstream of the primes. It does, but not evenly, and one of the four named candidates fails its own evidence. CONFIRMED as CHOKE_POINT with dated sources: solid rocket motors (six domestic suppliers to two between 2000 and 2015), projectile metal parts and forgings (named by Defense News as the limiting factor, with a $469 million purpose-built plant producing no conforming parts), seekers (one Boeing facility for every PAC-3 MSE radar seeker, 650 to 700 delivered in 2025), and energetic materials (one US RDX site, seven years to make an energetics line worker fully effective). NOT CONFIRMED: ammonium perchlorate. CSIS states that reliance on AMPAC alone is not currently a bottleneck because capacity outpaces demand by a significant margin, so it is mapped HIGH, as a disruption and price-setting risk, not as the gate. A map that had scored it CHOKE_POINT because the phrase sole source appears in the coverage would have been wrong on its best available source.

Crowdedness caution for the heat stage, recorded as a structural observation and not as a score. Solid rocket motors are the most cited bottleneck in this whole corpus of sources: CSIS wrote a report about it, SpaceNews and Breaking Defense covered that report, and the Pentagon announced a $3bn framework whose stated purpose is to widen it. That is the definition of a discovered constraint. The links that no fetched source treats as a story in itself are nozzle ablatives (rayon, where the supply problem is that defence demand alone cannot keep a commercial line open), nondestructive inspection and requalification (the mechanism that converts one supplier loss into a multi-year delay), and load, assemble and pack. Two of those three carry no listed exposure at all, which is itself the finding rather than a gap in the search.

Source dating note. The CSIS report cover shows JUNE 2026 with no day. The day used here, 2026-06-12, is taken from the publication's own filename on the CSIS server (260612_Rumbaugh_Rocket_Motors.pdf) rather than invented. The BAE Systems Holston article is dated 2013-01-05 and is cited only for the operator relationship and the product list, both of which the 2026 Modern War Institute piece independently corroborates for the single-site RDX claim. Two sources considered and NOT cited: the U.S. Army newsroom release on the domestic TNT contract returns HTTP 403, and CNBC's Rheinmetall propellant piece returns HTTP 403, so neither is evidence here and the TNT dependence claim rests on the Modern War Institute's Nitro-Chem contract figure instead.

Archetypes applied, from data/chains/_archetypes.md. ARCH-001 (precision manufacturing capacity as the gating step) fires twice and is the spine of this map: metal-parts-and-forgings and nondestructive-inspection are both capacity-and-qualification gates rather than product links. ARCH-003 (the uninvestable order-book owner) fires on dod-munitions-procurement, zero tickers, CHOKE_POINT, never the trade and always the schedule. ARCH-004 (critical material input, criticality set by substitutability times logistics) fires three times, on perchlorate-oxidizer, nozzle-ablatives and nitration-feedstocks, and its instruction to record both inputs is what kept ammonium perchlorate off CHOKE_POINT. ARCH-006 (geopolitical counter-response as a first-class link) fires on allied-rearmament-demand, wired in as a second sink competing for the same energetics and motors rather than left as narrative; the archetype library flags this one as the corpus's most likely systematic miss, and on this chain it is where the non-US exposure lives. ARCH-002 (EPC volume without capture) was CHECKED and does NOT fire: there is no competitively bid construction link on this map, and the closest analogue, load-assemble-pack, is government plant capacity rather than contractor volume. ARCH-007 (the semis layer as a leaf) was CHECKED and deliberately NOT included: GaN and RF microelectronics sit behind the radars that cue these interceptors, but no source fetched for this map ties a semiconductor constraint to the replenishment schedule, and an uncited link added to reach a round number is exactly what the citation bar exists to stop. ARCH-005 (power and grid equipment) does not apply to this occurrence.
